vignette:
Tariq Mansour is a 34-year-old Lebanese-American publisher who lives with his wife in a mid-sized city where he has built a modest but respected independent press over the past decade. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 74 and describes a period of profound psychological disruption that began approximately fourteen months ago, following a violent assault on his younger brother, Karim, who was attacked and severely beaten by a group of men while riding a city bus home late one evening. Tariq did not witness the assault directly, but arrived at the hospital within the hour, and it was there - in a fluorescent-lit corridor, with Karim barely conscious and a nurse pressing gauze to his face - that the full weight of what had happened landed on him. Karim survived, but sustained lasting injuries, and in the weeks that followed Tariq found himself unable to return to anything resembling his previous life.

What Tariq describes from that night is not a single coherent memory but something more like shattered glass: a fragment of Karim's swollen eye, the sound of a monitor beeping somewhere down the hall, his own voice saying his brother's name in a tone he did not recognise, and then nothing, and then the beeping again. These pieces do not assemble into a narrative. They arrive unbidden and out of sequence, sometimes as a kind of internal film that loops without resolution - the corridor, the gauze, the name - and sometimes as pure sound, the monitor's rhythm repeating in his head while he sits at his desk trying to read a manuscript. He has told his wife that he feels as though the night is still happening somewhere inside him, that it has not ended the way other experiences end.

In the months since, Tariq has reorganised his daily life around a set of precautions that feel to him entirely rational. He had come to believe, with a certainty that resists argument, that the world contains dangers he previously failed to notice. He now scans the faces of everyone who enters a room, reading micro-expressions and posture for signs of hostility, and he finds himself cataloguing objects - a letter opener on a colleague's desk, a wine bottle on a restaurant table - in terms of what harm they could do. He avoids any neighbourhood or venue he has not visited before, because an unfamiliar place is one whose threat level he cannot calculate in advance. This last habit has had concrete professional consequences: he declined to attend a book fair in another city, citing illness, and has twice sent a junior colleague to represent the press at events he would normally have led himself. His authors have begun to notice his absence, and one long-standing writer recently asked, carefully, whether everything was all right.

The bus is something he will not take. After Karim's assault, Tariq stopped riding public transit entirely. He drives everywhere now, adding sometimes forty minutes to his commute, and on the rare occasions when circumstances have placed him near a bus - waiting at a corner while one pulls in, the hydraulic hiss of its doors - he has felt something close to panic move through him without warning. He understands, on one level, that he is not Karim, and that the bus is not the same bus, but this understanding does not touch the feeling.

He has also noticed, with a shame he finds difficult to articulate, that moments of ordinary physical vulnerability have become intolerable. Undressing, the brief exposure of a shower - these produce a low, crawling alertness that he cannot switch off, as though being unguarded in body means being unguarded entirely. He is certain that he should be able to control this, and his inability to do so frightens him.

What finally brought Tariq to seek help was a conversation with his wife, who told him quietly one night that she felt she had lost access to him. He had not realised, until she said it, how completely he had withdrawn. He comes to therapy hoping, above all, to stop living inside that hospital corridor - and afraid, most of all, that he may not be able to.
